Definition (English): A stat that increases the damage dealt by reactions such as Blossom buds or Nova.
Every character deals one of six elements. A character’s element decides which reactions they can take part in.
The ring of six elements: Cosmos, Anima, Incantation, Chaos, Psyche and Lakshana. Elements next to each other on the ring react when both are applied to the same enemy.
A team gauge that fills during combat. Switching characters with a full meter applies the incoming character’s element and can set off a reaction.

Effects that refill or trigger the Esper Meter immediately, letting a team react far more often. Esper Zero and Blackbird do it with their Redirect Skills, so they don’t need Cycle Intensity to react quickly.
The effect created when two neighbouring elements meet on an enemy. There are six pair reactions and two trio reactions that need three neighbouring elements.
A stronger reaction that needs three neighbouring elements: Charge (Lakshana, Cosmos, Anima) or Discord (Incantation, Chaos, Psyche).

Blossom plants a Vita Bud, which fires Vita Pistils at nearby enemies for area damage. Several Espers change them: Jiuyuan adds Buds, Iroi makes copies, Nanally fires more Pistils, Mint widens their area, and Hotori keeps them attacking during Time Stop.
After Esper Cycle, plants a Vita Bud that blossoms into 5 Vita Pistils, which fly at nearby enemies and explode every 2s for area DMG. Up to 3 Vita Buds at once. Triggered by Cosmos + Anima.
The active character gains 10 extra Ultimate Energy when Vita Pistils (Blossom) hit a target in Remora. Needs Lakshana, Cosmos, Anima.
Removes part of the target’s Break bar while it has both Nova and Scorch. Needs Incantation, Chaos, Psyche.
For 12s after Esper Cycle, the target takes an extra follow-up attack equal to 20% of the Anima or Incantation DMG it takes. Triggered by Anima + Incantation.
Marks the target for 5s after Esper Cycle; when the mark ends, the target takes massive Mental DMG. Triggered by Chaos + Psyche.
Slows the target’s movement and attack speed for 5s after Esper Cycle. The slow fades over time and is shorter if reapplied. Triggered by Lakshana + Cosmos.
Burns the target with damage over time for 15s after Esper Cycle. Triggered by Incantation + Chaos.
The target takes 20% more Psyche and Lakshana DMG for 12s after Esper Cycle. Triggered by Psyche + Lakshana.

Also called: Affection Lv, Bond Level, Bond, Affinity
Definition (English): How close you are with an Esper. Gifts raise it: every gift gives some to anyone, and more to the Espers who favour it. Higher Bond Levels unlock City Hangouts (their story), Home Time invitations and, at Level 10, an outfit. Achievements ask for set levels too.
Raising a character’s level cap. Six ascensions take the cap from 20 to 80, each costing Beetle Coin, a tier of the character’s material family and their Anomaly Hunt boss drop.
Six optional upgrades (A1 to A6) for a character. Each duplicate copy unlocks one awakening slot, and you can turn on any awakenings up to that number, in any order or none at all.
A character’s HP, ATK and DEF before gear. This app lists Level 80 values without Arc or Console, as shown on the in-game character screen.
The currency spent on ascensions, skill upgrades and Arc upgrades. Taking one character from cap 20 to 80 costs 525,000.
Bond content for each Esper: City Hangouts is their own story, Home Time an invitation to your home. Both unlock with the Esper and enough Bond Level.
A person with supernatural abilities. Playable characters are Espers, each with a named Esper ability.

Also called: Character EXP, Arc EXP, Module EXP
Definition (English): Items that level things up: Character EXP for Espers, Arc EXP for Arcs and Module EXP for Console modules and Cartridges. Each comes in three tiers.
Each character ascends with one of four families (Whispers, Silhouette, Numeral or Delusions), used in three tiers as the level cap rises.
S-rank characters are the rarest; A-rank characters are more common and easier to fully upgrade.
Two bonuses per character that switch on automatically: R3 with 3 awakenings active and R6 with all 6. R3 usually raises skill levels; R6 is a bigger personal or team bonus.
A character’s ATK from their level plus their Arc’s ATK, before percentage bonuses. Team buffs “based on Base ATK” scale with this number, not with the character’s total ATK.
A character’s normal attack string, usually a five-hit combo (“Five-hit … combo” in skill text). Many change when held or after a dodge, and many build the character’s own resource as they hit.

Many characters build their own resource as they fight and spend it for stronger hits, such as Crime, Malice, Grain, Frames or String Energy. Each one only exists in that character’s kit; the Esper mechanics section explains how each is built and spent.

The four active skills every character has: Basic Attack, Redirect Skill, Ultimate and Support Skill. Each levels from 1 to 10 with skill cards and Beetle Coins, and some R3 Resonances add extra levels on top.
The wait before a skill or effect can be used again. Some awakenings shorten it, and some effects note their own cooldown, such as “(5s cooldown)”.
The named rule a character’s kit is built around, shown on the character page when the game spells it out.

Effects that “ignore X% DEF” skip that share of the target’s DEF for the hit: ignoring 20% means only the other 80% of its DEF reduces the damage, so the hit lands harder. It’s different from DEF shred, which lowers the enemy’s DEF itself for everyone attacking it.
How strong a hit is, given as a share of a stat, usually ATK. A hit that deals 200% ATK does twice the character’s ATK before other bonuses and the enemy’s DEF and RES.
An area some Ultimates create that stays for a while, such as Baicang’s Judgment of Autumn or Edgar’s Finnegan’s Wake. Effects inside it only work for enemies or allies in its range.
An enemy’s resistance to one element. Lowering it (RES Shred) raises the damage that element deals to them.
The game’s name for a character’s powers. The Esper Ability tab holds their skills and passives, and every character has a named ability of their own (shown as “Esper ability” on this app’s cards).
Being hit normally interrupts a character’s attack. Effects that grant hitstun immunity, or say an attack “isn’t interrupted”, let the character keep attacking through hits.
The on-field character is the one you’re controlling; the rest of the team is off-field. Some effects only work, or work better, while the character is off-field.
Two always-on effects per character, unlocked with skill cards. Passive 1 is usually the character’s Reaction Enhancement; Passive 2 is a personal or team bonus.
A passive that strengthens one or two reactions when the character takes part in them. This app tags those passives on each character page, and the Synergy score counts them.
A character’s main active skill, used on a cooldown between Basic Attacks. It often spends or builds the character’s own resource; Esper Zero’s and Blackbird’s also trigger Instant Cycle.
Effects that can apply several times, each adding the same bonus up to a cap. Text like “caps at 16” gives the cap; reapplying an effect that “refreshes” resets its timer instead of adding a stack.
A hit a teammate makes together with the active character, set up by Linko’s skills. Each one counts as the triggering character’s element, so it can feed reactions and element buffs.
An extra ability outside the combat skills and passives. Most are for exploring or city life, like gliding, flying or small gifts; a few, such as Hathor’s, also work in combat.
A character’s strongest skill, cast once their Ultimate Energy is full. Many Ultimates also give the character a stronger state for a few seconds.
The bar that unlocks a character’s Ultimate. It fills as they fight, and some skills, passives and awakenings grant it directly, to themselves or to teammates.

Adler’s shield (a barrier that soaks up damage before HP). Awakening A3 makes it 20% stronger, A4 absorbs the damage left over when it breaks, and A6 makes it last 12s. His R6 Resonance gives the whole team 10% Incantation DMG while they’re protected by it.

One of Zankou’s two Ultimates. Casting it inflicts Vile Ash on enemies and readies a free, enhanced Inferno Flamenco (her other Ultimate). With awakening A4 it casts automatically alongside Inferno Flamenco.

Aurelia’s empowered state from her Redirect Skill (Cadenza Aria): 12 seconds of stronger, wider jellyfish attacks. With awakening A2 she also enters it for 5s after a Critical Dodge (a last-moment dodge) or her Support Skill, and several awakenings add Crit Rate or Ultimate damage inside it.

Elyms’s link level: Weak, Medium or Strong. Her Redirect and Support Skills raise it. At Medium or Strong her Basic Attack becomes the stronger Crosstalk, and her Ultimate hits harder the stronger the link is, then resets it to Weak.
Aurelia’s Passive 2 stacks: each jellyfish blast that hits gives ATK +1% for 5s, up to 10 stacks. Awakening A6 raises the cap to 20 and grants 10 at once when she casts Cadenza Aria.

Chaos’s resource. His Basic Attack builds it, 30% faster on Warrant targets (enemies he has marked with Warrant) with awakening A1. Hold Basic Attack to spend it on Final Verdict, his finishing strike. His Ultimate puts him in Dread Echo, a state where he builds Crime fast, and awakening A6 refills it to the cap at once.

Fadia’s Basic Attack lets her take part of the damage meant for her teammates, and her Redirect Skill marks the highest-HP enemy so the damage she takes is reflected back at it. Awakening A1 raises the share she takes to 75%.

Shinku builds Defiant Spirit with her Basic Attack, Redirect Skill and Support Skill. Her Ultimate spends it to enter Surging Crimson, a state of heavy damage. Awakening A5 adds DEF and interrupt resistance (enemy hits are less likely to stop her attacks) in it, and R3 adds 30% damage.
The units Exe exports by spending Frames. His Basic Attack and Redirect Skill export them, and in Shader Compile (his Ultimate state) every attack can.
Elyms’s floating terminal. At Weak Connection it makes up to 5 Cosmos attacks with her Basic Attack (hold for Interference), and her Ultimate’s terminal deals area Cosmos DMG.
The state after Hathor’s Ultimate ride: extra speed and ATK, plus Crit DMG with awakening A6 and DEF ignore (part of the enemy’s DEF doesn’t count) with R6.

Haniel’s Redirect Skill deploys Hootie, a helper that buffs team ATK; Hootie’s stacks set off Ensemble, an area attack. Her Ultimate’s field (a lasting area) turns Ensemble into the stronger Symphony.

Hathor’s stacks, up to 6. She gets them from her Redirect Skill, from defeating enemies (Passive 2) and from her Rating Lock (enemies she has locked in place). With awakening A5 each stack adds 1% damage.

Skia’s shadow attacks that lock onto enemies, sent by his Basic Attack and made stronger by his Ultimate, The Pack. With Passive 1, a Fang Thrust that locks onto an enemy under Remora (slowed by the Remora reaction) applies Remora again.
With awakening A2, the Scorch (burn) and Hexed (follow-up) reactions on enemies build Flame Reserve, making the final hit of Zankou’s next Inferno Flamenco 150% stronger.
The mark Blackbird’s Redirect Skill puts on enemies. Her birds keep attacking marked enemies over time, so it’s damage that carries on while she does other things.

Exe’s resource. His attacks spend Frames to export Digital Echoes (units that fight for him): 10 Frames for one on his last Basic Attack hit, and up to 5 Echoes from his Redirect Skill depending on how many Frames he holds.

Chiz’s stock, like a currency she trades in battle. Her Basic Attack gains Grain on hit, holding her Redirect Skill spends it for extra damage, and her Ultimate opens the Grain Market, a state where her Redirect Skill cashes it in. Her awakenings play on the market theme: more storage, interest earned on a surplus and better chances of price rises.

The last hit of Zankou’s Basic Attack gives her Hunt. Awakening A1 makes Hunt permanent (+40% damage) and adds Delusion (+50% Crit DMG on the team’s DoT, damage over time). A3 adds interrupt resistance to Hunt and healing to Delusion.
Zankou’s Redirect Skill (Sanguine Dash) switches her to Illusion Form, applies Heartwrench to enemies and lowers their Break in an area.

Iroi’s resource, built by her lambs’ Basic Attack and her Support Skill. Her Ultimate’s dream gates heal or deal damage based on how much she has. With awakening A1 she regains it while off-field (not the character you’re controlling) and starts battles at max.

A debuff (a harmful effect on an enemy) from Daffodill’s Ultimate. With awakening A3 it stays and stacks up to 3; each stack then adds Break DMG (A4) and an extra Break hit (A5), where Break means emptying the enemy’s break bar to stagger them.
Stacks Adler builds with his Basic Attack. His A1 awakening gives 20 at once when he casts his Ultimate (Tranquility), and A2 turns each stack into 3% DMG Bonus (extra damage on everything he deals).

Edgar gets a Key (up to 3) each time he casts Wild Current (his Redirect Skill) or Weight of Knowledge (his Support Skill), and with awakening A1 whenever a teammate casts a Support Skill. Each Key makes Finnegan’s Vigil, the healing domain from his Ultimate, last 1s longer.

Sakiri’s partner. She rides Kiroumaru during her Basic Attack to eat weak enemies (up to 3 at once with awakening A6), and her Support Skill calls a giant Kiroumaru for area damage, DoT (damage over time) and DEF shred (lowering enemy DEF).

Jiuyuan’s mark. Her Basic Attack and Support Skill load Rose Pact Bullets, her Redirect Skill applies the Pact to enemies, and her Ultimate settles every Pact at once (Pact Settlement), exploding for damage. With Passive 2, Vita Pistils (from the Blossom reaction) also bind enemies with a Pact.
Fadia’s Ultimate state: she heals herself and her Basic Attacks become strong follow-up hits. Awakening A4 raises the healing and A5 adds 50% Crit Rate while she’s in it.

Blackbird’s resource. Her Basic Attack and Support Skill build it (Passive 2 adds 20 per Support Skill), and her bigger attacks spend it. With awakening A3, every attack that consumes Malice deals 50% more damage.

Shinku’s trait: standing still on the field for over 2s builds stacks (Critical Dodges, last-moment dodges, add more). Her next hit ends it with an Instant Strike worth +100% damage per stack. Awakening A3 lets it build while off-field, and A4 raises the cap to 16 with a stun at full stacks.

Linko’s Basic Attack builds Modulation, which powers Synced Strikes (teammates hitting together with the active character). Her Ultimate, Oversync, opens a Resonance Field, an area that syncs up to 3 allies and ends in a burst. R6 makes it last longer and boosts Anima and Incantation damage inside it.

Damage Lacrimosa stores on enemies with her Redirect Skill and Ultimate, released later. Awakening A1 makes it 50% stronger, A3 sets all of it off on her 5th Basic Attack hit, A4 makes it last 6s, and A5 means healing no longer removes it.

Stacks Elyms gains (15s each, up to 4) when Connection rises. Her enhanced Redirect Skill (Goodbye to You) spends them all for a higher DMG Ratio (a bigger multiplier on the hit) and raises Connection to Strong.

Two ways to use Akane’s Redirect Skill: tap it to mark one enemy with Overtone, or hold it to lay a Reverb Field (an area on the ground). Her Basic Attacks echo onto Overtone targets and enemies in the field (harder with awakening A5). With Passive 1, once the team first triggers Remora (the slowing reaction), she keeps reapplying it to both.
Haniel’s empowered form. While she’s in it her awakenings add Crit Rate (A3) and Psyche DMG (A5), R6 gives the team Crit DMG, and each Ensemble gives her 2 Plot Armor instead of 1.

Counter attacks that Daffodill’s Ultimate unlocks, up to 2. Passive 2 makes them 80% stronger, and with awakening A2 even a failed counter still Breaks the enemy (empties its break bar) and fully charges her Ultimate.

Haniel gains 1 for each Ensemble from the active character (the one you’re controlling), or 2 as Paranormal Ace, up to 4. It also raises how many times her Paranormal Cannon can bounce between enemies.

Words Baicang writes on the battlefield. Her Ultimate’s domain (a lasting area) creates them to deal damage or heal, and her Support Skill writes Silence, which with awakening A1 strengthens her next Skill. A Power Word that lands on a Scorched target (an enemy burning from the Scorch reaction) adds another Scorch. Awakening A2 gives ATK per Power Word and A3 lets her keep up to 4.

Exe’s combat grade: B, A, S, SS, then SSS. It climbs with his hits, skills, Ultimate, Support Skill, perfect dodges and counters, and every team Esper Cycle, and drains when he’s idle or gets hit. Higher Ratings earn Frames faster. His Passive 1 jumps it straight to SS when he triggers a Chaos Esper Cycle below SS.

Hathor’s trait: with her on the team, enemies that stay nearby for over 5s are locked (held in place) for 5s. If a locked enemy attacks the team the lock breaks and she gains 1 Express Delivery Power.

After her Ultimate, Elyms gets On the Line (six crystal icons under her portrait). While a teammate is on the field, she joins in with Remembrance follow-up attacks, single-target or area to match the Ultimate’s form, hitting harder the stronger her Connection was when she cast it.

Daffodill’s Redirect Skill is called Resonance. It gains a stack each time a teammate uses a Support Skill (the move they make when switched in), and at full stacks it becomes the faster Echoes. Not the same as the R3 and R6 Resonance bonuses every Esper has.
Exe’s Ultimate state: heavy area hits, and every attack can spend Frames to export Digital Echoes.
The state Akane’s Ultimate (Sonic Boom) starts. Casting the Ultimate again late in it lands a second, bigger hit.

Akane’s resource, up to 30, built by her Basic Attack. At 30 her Redirect Skill fires Synced Resonance, her big hit. Her R3 Resonance fills it when battle starts, and R6 gives 10 back after each Synced Resonance.

Adler’s phantoms. His Redirect Skill sends one charging in for area damage and DoT (damage over time) while shielding the active character (the one you’re controlling). His Ultimate summons five to strike every enemy.
Akane’s big Redirect Skill hit, fired at a full 30 String Energy. Her A1, A4 and R6 all trigger off it, giving her healing, defence or Crit DMG for the next 15–25s.

Hotori’s Redirect Skill spends her energy and records the Support and Redirect Skills her allies use. Her Ultimate stops time, replays everything recorded, then opens katana combos that end in a Finisher. With Passive 1, Vita Buds (from the Blossom reaction) keep attacking during Time Stop.

Nanally’s Ultimate calls Underboss to make follow-up attacks (extra hits that trigger on their own). In Ichi-daime’s Authority, she follows up herself whenever an ally deals Esper Cycle DMG (reaction damage), from Passive 2, and awakening A3 adds another follow-up on her own hits.

Chaos’s mark. His Redirect Skill puts it on up to 2 enemies and his Ultimate on everyone nearby. Warrant targets (marked enemies) take more damage, 30% with Passive 2. Awakening A2 ignores 20% of their DEF, A4 moves Warrant to a nearby enemy when a marked one dies, and R6 lowers their Lakshana RES (resistance) by 10%.

Blackbird’s Ultimate turns her into the Witch: heavy Psyche damage, an ATK buff for the team and hitstun immunity (enemy hits don’t interrupt her). Her Support Skill turns her into the Lonesome Bird for one strike that builds Malice.
Linko’s ghostly companion. Its arm launches her forward out of combat, and in a fight Xiaozhen hits an area and sets up synced strikes from her allies.
Tag for characters who help empty enemies’ break bars faster or make breaks deal more damage.
Characters who make the rest of the team stronger, for example by raising ATK, adding DMG bonuses, lowering enemy resistances or refilling Ultimate energy.
A damage dealer who does most of their damage in a short window, usually their Ultimate or an enhanced state, then swaps out.
Effects that limit what enemies can do: pulling them together, stunning, suppressing, knocking them into the air or slowing them. Most useful against groups; many bosses resist it.
Characters whose main job is dealing damage, either on the field for long stretches (Main DPS) or in short bursts when switched in (Burst DPS, Sub-DPS).
Tag for characters who raise the team’s damage directly, such as ATK buffs or DMG bonuses for allies.
Taking damage aimed at allies onto yourself, or turning damage taken into another resource, so the team survives longer.
An extra attack a character makes automatically after a condition is met, such as an ally’s skill or a set number of hits, without using a skill of their own.
Tag for characters who restore allies’ HP. Their healing usually scales with their HP or a Healing Bonus stat.
The character who stays on the field the longest and deals most of the team’s damage. Teams are usually built around them.
Fights up close. Melee characters usually need to stay near enemies and dodge well.
Lowering an enemy’s resistance to an element, so every hit of that element deals more damage. Works for the whole team.
Each character has an in-game role: Damage, Buff or Survival. Many cover more than one; the first listed is their in-game role and the others are how the community also uses them.
Tag for characters who protect allies with a barrier that absorbs damage. Shield strength usually scales with DEF or HP.
A secondary damage dealer who adds damage alongside the Main DPS, often off-field or through quick swap-ins, and frequently helps trigger reactions.

Characters who call extra units onto the field to fight beside the team, such as Exe’s Digital Echoes. Only Exe has the tag so far, but others summon too (like Control, which several Espers have without the tag): Nanally’s Underboss, Iroi’s lambs, Blackbird’s Forsaken Bird, Chaos’s Tindalos, Haniel’s Hootie and Adler’s Sunya. Some Arcs summon as well: Youthful Fantasy (the Black Tome), Camellia Society (from the Serenetti hunt) and Hethereau’s Keeper (Officer Whisker, from the Justice Executioner). So does the Blossom reaction, whose Vita Bud keeps firing on its own. A leak says Exe’s summon boosts will reach these too; not confirmed until his update.
Characters who keep the team alive with healing, shields or damage redirection, so the damage dealers can keep attacking.
The equipment slot that works like a weapon. An Arc adds base ATK, a secondary stat and a passive effect. Many S-rank characters have a signature Arc.
Extra copies of the same Arc strengthen its passive. M1 is a single copy; M5 is the maximum, with four duplicates.
An extra ability some Arcs unlock, like Officer Whisker, Silent Garden, Eclipse or the Black Tome. It works on its own timer once its condition is met.
Each character is compatible with one of five Arc types: Solid, Liquid, Gas, Plasma or Condensate (some sources call it Synthesis). Matching the type is required to equip an Arc.
A gear set. Equipping enough pieces of the same Cartridge set unlocks its 2-piece and 4-piece bonuses.
A character’s gear board. Modules are placed on it, and the Console grants traits based on how it is filled.
An item that stands in for missing copies of an Arc when raising its copies (M1 to M5).
A Cartridge has 1 main stat and 4 sub stats; a module has 2 main stats (flat ATK and HP) and 4 sub stats. Sub stats switch on at levels 5, 10, 15 and 20.
Shaped gear pieces placed on the Console, each carrying stats. Modules come in different types and shapes, such as vertical, L and Z pieces.
Modules come in sizes of 2, 3 and 4 squares (Type II, III and IV). Bigger types carry bigger stats, and each character gets a bonus for every module of one Type they equip.
A Cartridge set’s effect, unlocked when 2 and then 4 modules on the Console use one of that set’s four shapes.
The Arc made for a specific character, usually their best option. Some A-rank characters also have an S-rank signature, such as Haniel and Aurelia.
Raises how much a character’s hits fill enemies’ break bars and how hard breaks hit.
How quickly a character refills Ultimate energy. Higher values mean Ultimates come up more often.
How much extra damage a critical hit deals. Usually raised once CRIT Rate is high enough.
The chance for a hit to be a critical hit. Anything above 100% is wasted.

Also called: Basic Attack DMG, Ultimate DMG, Redirect Skill DMG, Esper Ability DMG, Attachment DMG, Mental DMG, Break DMG
Definition (English): Bonuses often only boost one kind of damage: Basic Attack, Redirect Skill or Ultimate DMG; Esper Ability DMG of one element; Break DMG; or the Attachment and Mental DMG some Espers’ attacks deal. A bonus only helps if the Esper deals that kind.
Increases damage of one element only. A common Cartridge main stat for damage dealers of that element.
Increases the healing a character gives. Healing Received Bonus increases the healing they get from others.
Increases all damage a character deals, whatever the element.
Enemies have a break bar. Emptying it staggers them and leaves them open to much higher damage for a short time.
Dodging at the last moment before an attack lands, when the enemy flashes red. You’re briefly invincible, and some characters follow it with a special counter attack, called a Critical Riposte.
Damage dealt in repeated ticks, such as Scorch. Some supports increase damage taken from each DoT on an enemy.
The move a character performs when switched in, often used to trigger reactions or apply buffs.
Cutting a move’s end lag short. The recovery at the end of a basic attack string can be cancelled with a dodge, a character swap or a parry, so you can act again sooner.
The counter attack from pressing Basic Attack right after a Critical Dodge. It hits hard, and some characters have their own version.
In action games, the game remembering a button pressed slightly early and doing it as soon as it can. How long NTE remembers presses hasn’t been documented yet.
Using a skill to parry an enemy attack. It also cancels that skill’s recovery, so it doubles as an animation cancel.
Switching characters just as an enemy attack lands: the incoming Esper parries it as their entry. The main defensive quick-swap trick.

A pulsing circle on a character’s portrait means they can be swapped in. Some characters change the rules: Mint needs more time on the field before she can swap out, and Esper Zero’s skill allows an instant swap.
When you switch characters, the incoming Esper attacks as they enter while the outgoing one is still finishing up. Depending on the character it’s a dash-in strike or an area burst.
A tabletop-RPG-style side mode added in 1.2, with its own classes, gear and difficulties.
Combat and puzzle missions picked up around the map, rewarding EXP, Annulith, Fons and materials. High-Risk Commissions are harder, timed versions that give Peril Hunt Medals.
Open-world bosses you can re-fight by spending Character Pixels. The main source of each character’s boss material for ascension, such as Tear of the Sea from Sea Prisoner.
Harder bosses such as Morphix (and Amber Broodmother from 1.5), claimable three times a week with Character Pixels, for advanced skill upgrade materials.
Stages that cost Character Pixels for upgrade materials: Houdinii’s Magic Stage (character EXP, Beetle Coin, Arc EXP), Houdinii’s Schemes (skill materials) and Bubble Can Factory (Arc ascension).

Train-themed endgame gauntlet of Stops. From the 6th Stop on, each Stop has Inbound and Outbound halves needing two teams with no character in common. Enemy weaknesses are shown in advance; faster clears earn up to 3 Seals.
Up to 4 players can explore a shared world, fight anomalies and play some city activities together. Story quests are single-player.
The collectibles auction: bid on lots, then show what you win in Collectibles Warehouse display cases, which earn passive income. Espers like Blackbird and Elyms can be your Auction Assistant.
Recurring limited event: a boss score attack where you raise difficulty and add modifiers for a higher score and more rewards.
Scratch cards. Fons won from them don’t count toward Tycoon Level or the Pawbes Rich List.
A 12-minute heist at the Pink Paws Bank: grab loot, avoid getting hit and escape in time for Fons and Paw-Paw Coins. Other players in your world can join. Chiz and Lacrimosa have life skills for it.
The Anomaly Zone for Console gear: it drops Cartridges and Carrota, which is spent on Rewind to roll modules.
A weekly 90-second damage race against the boss Mammon, paying Fons based on damage. Unlocked through Ebisu’s Auction House.

Also called: Circle Gifts, Pixel Surge, Stamina Recharge, Gold Clash, Fons Rush
Definition (English): Events that come back each version: Circle Gifts (log in 7 days for Solid Dice), Pixel Surge (double rewards for Character Pixels), Stamina Recharge and Fons Rush (double rewards for City Stamina in Hethereau Hobbies) and Gold Clash (double Fons in Pink Paws Heist).
A hide-and-seek multiplayer mode that costs City Stamina per round.
The rotating half of Beyond the Rails: 12 Stops that reset about every two weeks with a new buff. Each season is named after a Circle, such as Waxing or Fracture.

Also called: Bubble Can Factory, Houdinii’s Schemes, Houdinii’s Magic Stage
Definition (English): Anomaly Zones that cost Character Pixels: Bubble Can Factory drops Arc materials and Houdinii’s Schemes skill books; Houdinii’s Magic Stage is another.
Beach volleyball, added in 1.3: duo matches, multiplayer since 1.4 and a PvP rank system since 1.5. Weekly matches pay into the Tycoon Incentive Fund.
A currency earned from endgame modes, commissions and events.

Also called: Oddity, Bio Anomaly, Object Anomaly, Bureau of Anomaly Control
Definition (English): The strange phenomena Hunters deal with in Hethereau, and the creatures behind them. A Bio Anomaly is a person hosting an Oddity (like the Arbiter); an Object Anomaly is a thing come alive (like Teehee Bear). The Bureau of Anomaly Control looks after them, and most bosses are Anomalies.
What the game calls you, the player.

Also called: Arc banners, Limited Arc banner, Tri-Keys
Definition (English): The Arc banners. Each limited Esper comes with a limited Arc banner (“… Special”) alongside their own, pulled with Tri-Keys.
The Arc Exchange: a shop that sells Arcs, including the A-rank ones, for U-00NE, which anomaly bosses drop.
The in-game social app: posts, sharing and Bagel furniture and decor.
The energy spent on Anomaly Hunts, Anomaly Zones and weekly bosses. It refills over time.
The season pass. Playing raises your Bounty Rank for rewards; the paid track, Elite Hunter Supplies, lets you pick any S-rank Arc at Bounty Rank 30.
A separate weekly allowance spent on city activities for Fons. Unused points don’t carry over.

Also called: Illusion Town, Bridge Crossings, Miguel District, New Herland
Definition (English): Hethereau’s neighbourhoods. Shops, gift sellers and quests are listed by district, such as Illusion Town, Bridge Crossings, Miguel District and New Herland.
The item used, with Fons, to level up life skills. Bought from the Mall (the in-game shop) and earned from daily tasks.
Added in 1.3 with the Fogden Game story: Duskmoor is a new area, and Fogden the anomaly behind it.
Weekly auctions for collectibles, character materials and Arc items.
A Hunter Exchange item, bought with Fons, that substitutes for missing materials when upgrading Esper abilities or Arcs. Rarer materials take more Cores.
The city money earned from shops, minigames, heists and Realm of Greed. Also used for life skills.
The open-world city where NTE takes place.
City minigames such as Mahjong, racing, deliveries, Fight Club and fishing that spend City Stamina for Fons.
A shop paid in Fons that sells material selection boxes and Expansion Cores.
Your account level as a Hunter. It goes up as you play and unlocks more of the game; achievements ask you to reach set levels.
A character’s non-combat skill that helps with city activities, such as better shop prices or extra heist rewards.

How you get Espers: roll dice on a board. Limited boards (Solid Dice) feature one Esper for a few weeks; the Standard Board, Strange Encounters (Fabricated Dice), has the standard ones. Rolls count toward Perks milestones (at 50, 120 and 200), tracked per board.
The in-game shop: paid packs, plus items for Beetle Coins and other currencies, including Dreamless Seeds.

Also called: City Stamina Reserve, Photo Paper Supply
Definition (English): Since 1.5, City Stamina over the cap goes to the City Stamina Reserve and extra Character Pixels to the Photo Paper Supply, instead of being lost.
Homes you buy with Fons and decorate, like Stillmeadow House (1.3), where crops you grow sell for Fons. Figurines can stand anywhere on it.

Also called: Puka Stars, Pukaland Gold Pass, Puka Membership Program, Sweetdream Level
Definition (English): The amusement park added in 1.4. Puka Stars buy the Pukaland Gold Pass (90% off attractions for good), and the Puka Membership Program is its City Tycoon programme, with rewards by Sweetdream Level.
The character banners: where you pull for Espers. Limited Espers get their own board for a few weeks.

Also called: Anomaly, Character Esper, Arc Ascension and Anomaly Hunt Material Selection Boxes
Definition (English): Hunter Exchange boxes, bought with Fons (some also from the Circle Bounty), that let you pick one material: a tier-1 anomaly material, skill card or Arc material, or an Anomaly Hunt boss drop. Each Esper and Arc page lists which pick suits it.
A town at the foot of the mountains, added in 1.4 with The Witch story.
Cafe management: buy locations, set menus and assign staff for passive Fons. Some characters’ life skills improve it.
Your progress in city life, raised by earning Fons. Higher levels unlock activities such as cafes and Pink Paws Heist.
Cars and bikes for getting around Hethereau, bought with Fons or won from Mystery Box events, with liveries and tire effects to customise them. 1.5 added auto-drive.
A shop paid in Warp Pieces.
